title: AI limiting European workers' bargaining power, ECB's Lane says
source_used: BigGo Finance (account of the speech; Reuters text blocked)
key_facts: Philip Lane, chief economist of the European Central Bank (ECB), gave a speech in Dublin on 13 Oct.
He said expanding use of AI may be weakening workers' wage bargaining power and restraining wage growth.

He said AI's potential to substitute for some job categories could weaken workers' bargaining power, restrain wage growth and reduce the labour share of total income (BigGo's rendering, probably not verbatim).
He said AI is not fundamentally changing employment dynamics itself, but subdued corporate hiring plans limit workers' bargaining power as they seek pay to match high inflation.

He said heavy corporate borrowing worldwide to fund AI has pushed up long-term interest rates, significantly tightening financial conditions in the euro area, an important factor in the ECB's policy stance.
Over the longer term he said AI could raise potential growth and offset the effect of a shrinking working-age population.
BigGo adds that euro-area inflation is running at nearly double the ECB's 2% target on surging energy prices and that policymakers see no second-round wage effects yet.
quote_evidence: ECB Chief Economist Philip Lane said in a speech in Dublin on the 13th that the expanding use of AI may be weakening workers' wage bargaining power and restraining wage growth.
He also noted that massive borrowing by companies worldwide to fund AI investments has pushed up long-term interest rates, significantly tightening financial conditions in the Eurozone.
He expressed the view that over the longer term, AI could boost potential growth and offset the economic impact of a shrinking working-age population.
why_it_matters_hint: The ECB's chief economist names AI as a possible drag on pay and as a force tightening borrowing conditions in Europe.
notes: Reuters page blocked (401). BigGo Finance's account of the same speech was read instead; BigGo looks machine-translated, so its quotations are paraphrased in the entry and the Reuters headline carries the main claim. The ECB's own speech text was not opened.
